newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch insurance body sees few Jewish war claims.
newsitem.headline: Dutch insurance body sees few Jewish war claims.

text.p: The Dutch insurers association said on Wednesday it was not expecting its members to receive many claims from relatives of Jewish World War Two victims who held policies concluded before or during the war.

Earlier this week Dutch insurer Aegon said it was willing to settle with a next-of-kin of a pre-war life policy holder killed in a Nazi concentration camp, adding it was offering over 50,000 guilders.
"We think it will be all right," an insurers association spokeswoman said. The body had started looking at the issues surrounding such claims in March this year she said.
Delta Lloyd, a unit of Britain's Commercial Union, confirmed on Wednesday it was also handling a comparable case.
Delta Lloyd said it was investigating a request from a relative of one of their possible Jewish former life insurance policy holders killed during the war.
"We are investigating a claim at the moment," a spokesman said. He declined to say how much money could be involved with the claim.
Other big insurers in the Netherlands, Fortis Amev and Nationale-Nederlanden, a unit of ING, said they had not currently received similar requests from relatives of war victims.

The Netherlands, following turmoil about Swiss wartime dealings, recently established commissions to look at the fate of assets belonging to Dutch Jews caught up in the Holocaust during the country's occupation by the Nazis in World War Two.
The commissions are expected to report in a few months' time, the insurers association said.

Insurers liabilities are expected to be limited by a 1954 agreement with the Dutch state in terms of which all monies from such unclaimed policies were put into a central fund, with the state assuming liability.
